PETITION FOR LEGAL SEPARATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Pat Morgan · Jordan Lee

DECLARATION OF PARTIES, MARRIAGE DATE, AND PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Petition for Legal Separation — Information Sheet concerns the marriage of Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee, who were married on June 12, 2015 and identify March 1, 2026 as their date of separation. It is prepared for use alongside an actual petition for legal separation of the parties that would be filed in the California superior court for Sacramento County. As California's Family Code recognizes, a petition seeking to end or alter a marriage's legal status may instead seek dissolution of the marriage or a judgment of nullity — two other, distinct proceedings addressed in this corpus's separate Petition for Dissolution of Marriage (Divorce) — Information Sheet and Nullity of Marriage (Annulment) — Petition Information Sheet documents, not restated here. This information sheet describes what is distinctive about legal separation as its own statutory proceeding — that it has no residency requirement to file, that a resulting judgment does not end the parties' marital status, and how it relates procedurally to dissolution — as background for that filing. It is not itself a court filing, and completing it does not legally separate, dissolve, or otherwise change the marital status of Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee. Only a court judgment can do that.

NO RESIDENCY OR DURATIONAL REQUIREMENT TO FILE FOR LEGAL SEPARATION — UNLIKE DISSOLUTION
California's Family Code imposes a residency requirement on dissolution that it does not impose in the same terms on legal separation. A judgment of dissolution of marriage may not be entered unless one of the parties has been a resident of California for six months and a resident of the county where the proceeding is filed for three months, both periods measured immediately before the petition is filed. The statute governing amendment of a legal separation proceeding confirms, by its own terms, that this residency requirement does not likewise gate a legal separation filing: it expressly contemplates "a proceeding for legal separation of the parties in which neither party, at the time the proceeding was commenced, has complied with the residence requirements of Section 2320," and provides that once a party later does comply with those requirements, that party may amend the petition or responsive pleading to instead request a judgment of dissolution — with the amendment's filing date deemed the commencement date of the dissolution proceeding for residency purposes only. California's official courts self-help website describes the same distinction in plain language: to file for a legal separation, only one spouse must live in California, and "There's no time requirement," while a divorce filing requires one spouse to have lived in California for the past six months and in the filing county for at least three months.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Except as provided in subdivision (b), a judgment of dissolution of marriage may not be entered unless one of the parties to the marriage has been a resident of this state for six months and of the county in which the proceeding is filed for three months next preceding the filing of the petition."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2320(a) (California Legislative Information text), the six-month state / three-month county residency requirement, stated only for a judgment of dissolution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2320.)
  "In a proceeding for legal separation of the parties in which neither party, at the time the proceeding was commenced, has complied with the residence requirements of Section 2320, either party may, upon complying with the residence requirements, amend the party’s petition or responsive pleading in the proceeding to request that a judgment of dissolution of the marriage be entered."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2321(a) (California Legislative Information text), a legal separation proceeding filed without compliance with the residence requirements, and amendment to dissolution once they are met (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2321.)
  "only one spouse must live in California. There's no time requirement."
  — California Courts Self-Help Guide, "Legal separation" (courts.ca.gov), only one spouse must live in California to file for legal separation, with no time requirement (https://selfhelp.courts.ca.gov/divorce-california/legal-separation)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute and its own self-help publication, used as real evidence of California's legal-separation process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage. This document is informational: it does not itself determine whether either party satisfies any residency requirement, or whether amending a specific petition from legal separation to dissolution would be proper; only a court can make that determination. The two Family Code citations are to two different sections (§ 2320 and § 2321), and are independent of each other; the California Courts self-help page is a separate, non-statutory source independent of both, though its own two quoted sentences come from the same single web page and are not independent of one another. This clause's first sentence characterizes § 2320 as not imposing a residency requirement on legal separation "in the same terms"; that characterization rests on § 2320(a)'s own text, which speaks only of "a judgment of dissolution of marriage," and on § 2321(a)'s express contemplation of a legal-separation proceeding filed without compliance with § 2320 — not on any statute that affirmatively states legal separation has no residency requirement in so many words. Section 2320(b), a same-sex-marriage residency exception, does expressly extend to legal separation and is addressed in this corpus's companion dissolution document rather than restated here. Section 2321(b), governing notice of such an amendment, was read but is not quoted here.

A JUDGMENT OF LEGAL SEPARATION DOES NOT END MARITAL STATUS
California's Family Code gives dissolution, but not legal separation, a dedicated statutory statement of what its judgment does to the parties' marital status: the Family Code's chapter titled "Effect of Dissolution" — consisting of a single section — states that "the effect of a judgment of dissolution of marriage when it becomes final is to restore the parties to the state of unmarried persons." No parallel Family Code chapter gives a judgment of legal separation that same status-restoring effect. Consistent with that statutory structure, California's official courts self-help website states the practical consequence in plain terms: in a legal separation, "you stay married," and "When it's final, you are still legally married" — with the further, related consequence that a party who has legally separated "can't marry or enter into a domestic partnership with someone else." A legal separation proceeding can still result in the same kinds of financial and parenting orders as a dissolution — division of property and debts, spousal or domestic partner support, and child custody, visitation, and support — addressed in a separate clause of this document; what it does not do is change either party's marital status.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The effect of a judgment of dissolution of marriage when it becomes final is to restore the parties to the state of unmarried persons."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2300 (California Legislative Information text), a judgment of dissolution restores the parties to unmarried status, in a chapter captioned solely "Effect of Dissolution" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2300.)
  "When it's final, you are still legally married"
  — California Courts Self-Help Guide, "Legal separation" (courts.ca.gov), the parties remain legally married after a final judgment of legal separation, and cannot remarry (https://selfhelp.courts.ca.gov/divorce-california/legal-separation)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute and its own self-help publication, used as real evidence of California's legal-separation process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage. This document is informational: it does not itself enter a judgment of legal separation or determine any party's marital status; only a court judgment does that. The Family Code citation (§ 2300) and the California Courts self-help page are independent, non-overlapping sources; the self-help page's own three quoted phrases come from the same single web page and are not independent of one another. This clause's statement that no parallel Family Code chapter restores unmarried status upon legal separation is an inference from the structure of Division 6, Part 3 of the Family Code — specifically, that Chapter 1, captioned "Effect of Dissolution" and spanning only Section 2300, addresses solely dissolution's effect — rather than a claim independently verified against every other chapter of that Part; this document's research did not exhaustively review every section of Division 6 to confirm no other provision addresses legal separation's status effect.

THE SAME NO-FAULT GROUNDS AND COMMUNITY-PROPERTY DEFAULT APPLY TO LEGAL SEPARATION AS TO DISSOLUTION
Rather than maintaining a separate substantive framework, California's Family Code repeatedly folds legal separation into the same statutory rules it applies to dissolution, stating each rule for both proceedings in a single sentence. The two available grounds are shared and stated together: "Dissolution of the marriage or legal separation of the parties may be based on either of the following grounds, which shall be pleaded generally" — irreconcilable differences causing the irremediable breakdown of the marriage, or permanent legal incapacity to make decisions — the same two no-fault grounds, defined the same way, addressed more fully in this corpus's companion dissolution document rather than restated here. Property division follows the same pattern: absent the parties' written agreement, their oral stipulation in open court, or another statutory exception, the court "shall, either in its judgment of dissolution of the marriage, in its judgment of legal separation of the parties, or at a later time if it expressly reserves jurisdiction to make such a property division, divide the community estate of the parties equally" — one statute, naming both judgment types side by side, governing the community-property default for either proceeding alike.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Dissolution of the marriage or legal separation of the parties may be based on either of the following grounds, which shall be pleaded generally: (a) Irreconcilable differences, which have caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage. (b) Permanent legal incapacity to make decisions."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2310(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), the same two no-fault grounds stated for both dissolution and legal separation in one sentence (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2310.)
  "the court shall, either in its judgment of dissolution of the marriage, in its judgment of legal separation of the parties, or at a later time if it expressly reserves jurisdiction to make such a property division, divide the community estate of the parties equally"
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2550 (California Legislative Information text), the equal community-property division default, applied by name to a judgment of legal separation as well as dissolution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2550.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's legal-separation process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage. This document is informational: it does not itself determine grounds, divide property, or order support or custody in any specific case; only a court can do that. The two citations are to two different Family Code sections (§ 2310 and § 2550), and are independent of each other. This clause addresses only the grounds and the community-property default; it does not restate this corpus's companion dissolution document's fuller treatment of those same two statutes (including § 2311's definition of irreconcilable differences and § 2312's proof standard for legal incapacity), and it does not independently verify the spousal-support or child-custody statutes, which this document's research did not separately confirm apply to legal separation by their own text in the way § 2310 and § 2550 do — a reader should not assume every dissolution-related statute extends to legal separation without checking that statute's own language.

NO SIX-MONTH WAITING PERIOD, AND COMMONLY CITED REASONS FOR CHOOSING LEGAL SEPARATION
Just as the residency requirement is stated only for dissolution, so is the Family Code's mandatory waiting period: subject to a small set of statutory exceptions, "no judgment of dissolution is final for the purpose of terminating the marriage relationship of the parties until six months have expired" from service of the petition or the respondent's appearance, whichever occurs first — a rule addressed more fully in this corpus's companion dissolution document. California's official courts self-help website confirms that legal separation has no counterpart to that wait: describing the six-month period as running to when a couple can divorce, it states, "There isn't one for a legal separation." The same source identifies reasons some spouses choose legal separation over dissolution: "Some couples don't want to get divorced for religious reasons, personal beliefs, or financial reasons. For example, they stay married to keep a spouse or domestic partner on an insurance or benefit plan." It also notes that a spouse who wants a divorce but has not yet met dissolution's residency requirement may file for legal separation first and later amend to seek dissolution, and states, "You can usually change a legal separation to a divorce" if the case is not yet final — consistent with the amendment mechanism in Family Code § 2321 addressed in a separate clause of this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "no judgment of dissolution is final for the purpose of terminating the marriage relationship of the parties until six months have expired from the date of service of a copy of summons and petition or the date of appearance of the respondent, whichever occurs first"
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2339(a) (California Legislative Information text), the six-month waiting period, stated only for a judgment of dissolution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2339.)
  "Some couples don't want to get divorced for religious reasons, personal beliefs, or financial reasons. For example, they stay married to keep a spouse or domestic partner on an insurance or benefit plan."
  — California Courts Self-Help Guide, "Legal separation" (courts.ca.gov), no six-month wait for legal separation, common reasons for choosing it, and the path to later amend to a divorce (https://selfhelp.courts.ca.gov/divorce-california/legal-separation)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute and its own self-help publication, used as real evidence of California's legal-separation process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage. This document is informational: it does not itself waive any waiting period or determine why any specific party is choosing legal separation; only a court proceeding resolves a specific case, and the reasons stated here are commonly cited background drawn from California's own self-help publication, not a statement of any specific party's motivation or of settled case law. The Family Code citation (§ 2339) and the California Courts self-help page are independent, non-overlapping sources; the self-help page's several quoted phrases come from the same single web page and are not independent of one another. Section 2339(a) itself cross-references further exceptions (Sections 2340 to 2344) that this document's research did not independently fetch or verify, consistent with this corpus's companion dissolution document's treatment of the same statute.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT — NOT A COURT FILING
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct.

Executed on September 2, 2026 at Sacramento, California.

Signature of Pat Morgan: ☐ _________________________
